- If sentiment is consistently negative (0.00 or low) over recent days, model tends to underpredict — adjust forecast upward by 2–5% to account for bearish sentiment’s lagged effect.
- If sentiment is consistently positive (1.00 or high) and model is trending flat or downward, model is overly pessimistic — adjust upward by 3–7% to reflect bullish sentiment momentum.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model often overshoots and continues upward — cap forecast at 1–2% below recent peak or use moving average of last 5 days to prevent overcorrection.
- When sentiment is neutral (0.33–0.67) and model is trending downward, model may be overreacting — consider mean reversion to 10–15% above recent 10-day average.
- If model forecast is consistently below true outcome (e.g., 30d forecast < 80, true > 85), model is underestimating bullish momentum — increase forecast by 5–10% if sentiment is positive or volatile.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome (e.g., 30d forecast > 85, true < 80), model is overestimating — reduce forecast by 5–10% if sentiment is negative or stagnant.
- For 30d horizon, if true outcome shows strong upward trend after 10–15 days, model often fails to capture momentum — add 1–3% per day of momentum (e.g., 3% after 10 days) if sentiment is positive.
- If sentiment history shows sudden shift from negative to positive (e.g., 0.00 → 1.00), model often lags — adjust forecast 2–5 days ahead to reflect sentiment change.
